title: Hyper-V Live Migration Failure and Long-Blackout Events
exclusions: Reports only Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-VMMS/Admin event 21502, which Microsoft documents across multiple live-migration failure conditions, and event 20417, which documents a completed live migration with an unexpectedly long blackout. It does not enumerate every migration, prove a normal migration succeeded, calculate migration duration or downtime, identify the cause from EventCode alone, or cover quick migration, storage-only moves, failover-cluster ownership changes, guest application availability, post-move network reachability, or silent telemetry loss. Message text and optional event payload fields vary by Windows build and locale; responders must inspect the raw event and corroborating host, cluster, network, storage, authentication, VM, and guest evidence. The local index, schedule, source type, and exception lookup are deployment conventions. This UC does not start, retry, cancel, or remediate a migration.
evidence: After deployment, retain the saved-search definition `hyperv_live_migration_failure_or_long_blackout`, ACL, five-minute schedule, dispatch rows, triggered alerts, and throttle state; effective WinEventLog input and deployment assignment; raw VMMS/Admin records with EventCode, provider, channel/source, host, event record identity, time/index time, level, rendered message, and XML when enabled; `hyperv_live_migration_event_exceptions.csv` revisions; source-health and control-test results; Failover Cluster Manager or Hyper-V Manager job context; relevant cluster, VMMS, Worker, network, storage, authentication, and guest-availability evidence; incident disposition; and a later approved successful migration or corrective validation. These artifacts show the two recorded VMMS conditions and search behavior, not complete migration accounting or application continuity. This documentation-only review created no migration, event, search, alert, outage, or production evidence.

controlTest.positiveScenario: Fix dispatch at 2026-07-29T01:00:00Z and use an isolated fixture index/source type. Ingest one VMMS/Admin event at 00:56 from `hv-lab-01` with provider `Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-VMMS`, EventCode=21502, EventRecordID=401, and a failure message; ingest one event at 00:57 from `hv-lab-02` with EventCode=20417, EventRecordID=509, and a message containing an unexpectedly long blackout time of 12.4 seconds. With no active exception, expect exactly two rows: `migration_failed` with severity `high` and `migration_completed_long_blackout` with severity `medium`, preserving the distinct record identities and raw messages.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Run isolated variants and require zero rows for VMMS/Admin EventCode 21024, a VMMS Operational record with EventCode 21502, a Worker/Admin error, an event outside the closed ten-minute range, and either target event with an exact host/event-code exception whose numeric expiry is after dispatch and whose reason, ticket, and owner are nonempty. An exception expiring exactly at dispatch, malformed exception, or exception for another host/code must not suppress. Duplicate copies with the same host, event code, and EventRecordID must collapse to one row; distinct EventRecordID values must remain distinct.

dataSources: Windows Event Log channel `Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-VMMS/Admin` from every in-scope Hyper-V host, collected by a supported Splunk Windows event-log input. This UC targets the non-XML local source type `WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-VMMS-Admin`; deployments using `renderXml=true` commonly receive an `XmlWinEventLog:` source type and must qualify equivalent field extraction before changing the search. Microsoft identifies VMMS/Admin and Worker/Admin as live-migration diagnostic logs and documents Event IDs 21502 and 20417. Required fields are `_time, _indextime, host, source|channel, sourcetype, EventCode, EventRecordID|RecordNumber|_cd, Message`, with provider, level, and XML payload retained when available. `index=wineventlog` and the exception lookup are local conventions.
app: Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (Splunkbase 742) plus a deployment-owned input/search app. The archived Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Hyper-V 4.0.0 documents the exact VMMS/Admin source type but is not presented as a current dependency. Native Splunk WinEventLog collection can collect the channel; the deployment must validate source-type spelling and extraction on its supported Windows, forwarder, and add-on versions.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-VMMS-Admin" EventCode IN (20417,21502) earliest=-10m@m latest=@m
| eval event_code=tonumber(EventCode), event_uid=coalesce(EventRecordID,RecordNumber,_cd), finding=case(event_code=21502,"migration_failed",event_code=20417,"migration_completed_long_blackout"), severity=case(event_code=21502,"high",event_code=20417,"medium")
| where isnotnull(finding) AND len(event_uid)>0
| dedup host event_code event_uid
| lookup hyperv_live_migration_event_exceptions.csv host event_code OUTPUT exception_until_epoch reason AS exception_reason ticket exception_owner
| eval exception_until_epoch=tonumber(exception_until_epoch), exception_active=if(exception_until_epoch>now() AND len(exception_reason)>0 AND len(ticket)>0 AND len(exception_owner)>0,1,0)
| where exception_active=0
| eval observation_semantics="vmms_admin_21502_failure_or_20417_completed_with_unexpected_long_blackout_not_complete_migration_accounting", use_case_id="UC-2.2.4"
| table _time _indextime host event_code event_uid finding severity Message provider source sourcetype observation_semantics use_case_id
| sort 0 -_time host event_uid
description: Runs every five minutes over the previous ten closed minutes and returns one row per distinct Hyper-V VMMS/Admin event 21502 or 20417. Event 21502 is labelled a live-migration failure; event 20417 is labelled a completed migration with an unexpectedly long blackout. Host, record identity, message, and timing remain available for investigation.
value: Live-migration failures can block maintenance or workload balancing, while a long blackout can violate availability expectations even when the move completes. Fast, record-level routing lets virtualization teams distinguish recurring destination, compatibility, authentication, network, storage, and capacity problems and preserve the native evidence needed for Microsoft-supported troubleshooting.
implementation: Collect `Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-VMMS/Admin` from every governed Hyper-V host with a supported Windows event-log input, retaining EventCode, event record identity, message, provider/channel, event time, and index time. Validate source-type and field extraction on each Windows/forwarder/add-on cohort. Save the SPL with a ten-minute closed lookback on a five-minute schedule; alert once per event identity and inspect the raw record rather than treating 21502 as one root cause. Maintain only exact, expiring host/event-code exceptions. Pair the alert with VMMS/Worker, cluster, network, storage, authentication, VM configuration, and guest checks; never automate migration retry from Splunk.
visualization: Put collection trust first: VMMS/Admin freshness by expected host, host coverage, source-type variants, null EventCode/record identity/message rates, indexing delay, and duplicate record identities. Then show counts by finding, host, EventCode, hour, and change window; a timeline of failures versus long-blackout completions; top recurring raw error codes/message fingerprints; and an event table with direct raw-event drilldown. Link to Failover Cluster Manager or Hyper-V Manager context and companion network, storage, host-capacity, and guest-availability panels. Do not label the absence of these two IDs as successful migration health.
dataModelAcceleration: Not applicable. No accelerated CIM dataset is asserted to preserve the native VMMS provider/channel, Event IDs 21502 and 20417, event record identity, rendered message/XML payload, or their Microsoft troubleshooting semantics. Raw Windows Event Log records remain primary.

knownFalsePositives:
A result is a real VMMS/Admin record with one of the two documented IDs. The likely benign cases concern operational intent or duplicate collection, not denial that Windows recorded the condition.

1. **Approved migration compatibility test** — A virtualization engineer may deliberately reproduce a 21502 condition in a lab or maintenance window. Confirm exact source/destination hosts, VM, operator, change/test ID, expected failure, start/end, and raw error. Use an exact host/event-code exception only for the bounded test window; do not suppress a production cluster or all migration failures.

2. **Planned host drain or patch cycle exposes an existing mismatch** — Maintenance can generate repeated 21502 events while a bad destination, switch, CPU/configuration version, authentication, or capacity condition is discovered. Correlate Failover Cluster Manager actions, drain owner, target node, patch/change, and raw VMMS/Worker/cluster evidence. The failure remains actionable even when the migration was planned.

3. **Accepted long blackout during a measured stress exercise** — Event 20417 may be expected while testing constrained bandwidth, high dirty-page workload, compression, SMB, or simultaneous migration settings. Verify the approved performance test, measured blackout objective, VM criticality, source/destination, guest probe, and end time. A test exception must be exact and expiring.

4. **Duplicate event collection** — Two forwarders, Windows Event Forwarding plus local collection, or duplicate input assignments can index the same native record more than once. Compare host, provider, channel, EventRecordID, `_cd`, source, forwarder, and `_indextime`. The SPL collapses exact host/code/record identity in one dispatch, but collection-health must expose and remove duplication.

5. **Late arrival overlaps schedules** — The ten-minute lookback intentionally overlaps five-minute dispatches. Alert throttling by host/event identity prevents duplicate notification while preserving the event on dashboards. Validate event-time/index-time delay and scheduler behavior; do not reduce the range until measured ingestion delay supports it.

6. **Restored migration after an initial failure** — A later successful move does not make the earlier 21502 false. Link both outcomes to one incident/change, verify destination ownership and guest/application health, and close with evidence rather than deleting or suppressing the failure record.

**Suppression mechanism:** the `hyperv_live_migration_event_exceptions.csv` lookup matches exact `host,event_code` and requires a future numeric `exception_until_epoch`, nonempty reason, ticket, and exception owner. It applies after native event validation. Expired/malformed exceptions, another host or code, source-health failure, duplicate collection, and unreviewed production failures remain visible.
reviewer: documentation-only Cursor AI editorial review against primary Microsoft Hyper-V live-migration troubleshooting, setup, event-log, and PowerShell guidance plus Splunk Windows Event Log, scheduled-alert, current Windows add-on, and archived Hyper-V source-type documentation; Windows/Hyper-V/cluster/forwarder/add-on/Splunk versions, event payloads and localization, collection, fields, SPL, fixtures, exceptions, alerting, migration behavior, guest impact, and production response were specified but not executed or Microsoft/Splunk/virtualization/workload-owner/SME signed
detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and exact claim boundary

Assign Hyper-V, Failover Clustering, Windows, network, storage, identity/Active Directory, Splunk data/content, workload, and incident/change owners. Inventory every in-scope source and destination host, cluster, VM criticality, live-migration network and performance option, authentication mode, storage path, switch identity, Windows build, VM configuration version, forwarder/add-on assignment, and runbook. The search role needs the Windows-event index, lookup read, scheduling, and approved notification rights; restrict input and exception writes.

Microsoft defines live migration as moving a running VM between hosts with minimal downtime. Microsoft also documents many distinct causes under Event ID 21502 and separately states that VMMS event 20417 means the service completed a live migration with an unexpectedly long blackout. Therefore, EventCode alone supports only the labels in this UC. It does not support a universal root cause, normal-completion ledger, exact duration, or application-availability claim. Preserve and inspect the native message, payload, host context, and related logs.

This review did not run any Windows, Hyper-V, cluster, forwarder, add-on, or Splunk version. Do not retain the former `splunkVersions` assertion. The archived Splunk Hyper-V add-on documents the non-XML `WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-VMMS-Admin` source type, but the current implementation uses supported Windows event-log collection and local qualification. If XML rendering is enabled, use the observed `XmlWinEventLog:` source type and map equivalent fields in a tested variant; do not search both spellings without verifying duplicate behavior.

## Step 1 — Configure and prove VMMS/Admin collection

On each Hyper-V host, verify the channel with Event Viewer under Applications and Services Logs > Microsoft > Windows > Hyper-V-VMMS > Admin or with approved `Get-WinEvent -LogName "Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-VMMS/Admin"`. Microsoft also recommends Worker/Admin, cluster logs, network diagnostics, VM/configuration, switch, and processor information for live-migration troubleshooting; collect those as companion evidence, not as undocumented fields in this primary rule.

Deploy the supported Splunk Windows event-log input to every governed host. A non-XML local stanza is conceptually:

```ini
[WinEventLog://Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-VMMS/Admin]
disabled = 0
index = wineventlog
renderXml = 0
```

Confirm exact syntax against the deployed Splunk release. `index=wineventlog` and the resulting source type are local choices. If `renderXml=true`, Splunk documents that XML allow/deny filtering requires `$XmlRegex`; validate event boundaries, source type, EventCode, provider/channel, EventRecordID, message/payload, host, event time, index time, and localization before filtering at ingest. Avoid an ingest allowlist of only two IDs until retention requirements and future troubleshooting needs are approved.

For each host/build/locale cohort, generate no production failure merely for testing. Find existing approved records or use a lab migration exercise. Compare Splunk raw output with Event Viewer/Get-WinEvent for EventCode, record ID, timestamp, provider, channel, level, XML/rendered message, and host. Measure indexing delay and verify host identity survives Windows Event Forwarding or intermediate collection.

Create `hyperv_live_migration_event_exceptions.csv` with exact `host,event_code,exception_until_epoch,reason,ticket,exception_owner`. Reject wildcard hosts, absent owners, unsupported codes, duplicate keys, and indefinite expiry. Separately monitor expected-host channel freshness, disabled logs/inputs, forwarder health, duplicate input assignments, null record identity, source-type drift, and indexing lag. Missing events are not proof of healthy migrations.

## Step 2 — Save and understand the event-level SPL

Save the sidecar SPL as `hyperv_live_migration_failure_or_long_blackout`. Run every five minutes with aligned `earliest=-10m@m latest=@m`; the closed boundary avoids partially indexed current-minute data and the overlap tolerates measured delay. The base search fixes the exact non-XML source type and only EventCodes 20417 and 21502. `event_uid` prefers the native EventRecordID, then RecordNumber, then Splunk `_cd`; a row without any identity is rejected and reported by source-health.

The `case` mapping intentionally has only two outcomes. Event 21502 becomes `migration_failed` and local severity high. Event 20417 becomes `migration_completed_long_blackout` and local severity medium. Severity is routing policy, not a Microsoft level conversion. `dedup host event_code event_uid` removes same-dispatch duplicate copies but preserves distinct repeated failures. The lookup applies only after event qualification and requires complete active governance fields.

Trigger once for each `host,event_code,event_uid` and throttle that identity longer than the overlap, such as 30 minutes. Do not throttle all failures for a host into one opaque alert; aggregate repeated events into an incident while retaining every native record. Include the raw message, times, provider/source, and drilldowns. A 21502 should open or update a migration-failure incident; 20417 should route according to VM criticality and blackout objectives after identifying the VM from the raw payload/job context.

Avoid message regex as the primary identity because message wording and insertion fields vary by build and locale. If the deployment extracts VM ID/name, destination host, error code, or blackout seconds from XML, document the exact event schema for every supported cohort and add null/schema-drift tests. Until then, display those values only when confidently extracted and keep Message authoritative.

## Step 3 — Validate controls, boundaries, and observability

Use fixed-time isolated fixtures and substitute only the fixture index/source type. Run the positive control and assert two exact records, labels, severities, times, and messages. Run every negative independently. Add cases for EventCode as string/integer, null/malformed code, EventRecordID fallback order, same record arriving twice, different records with identical messages, host case policy, XML source type, provider mismatch, index delay, and exception expiry at one second before/equal/after dispatch.

In a nonproduction Hyper-V pair or cluster, coordinate an approved migration test. Capture source/destination host settings, VM state, Move-VM or Failover Cluster Manager job, VMMS/Admin and Worker/Admin events, cluster log if applicable, network/storage metrics, and guest probe. If engineering intentionally produces a known 21502 condition, restore configuration and prove a later approved migration plus guest health. Do not corrupt checkpoints, remove switches, exhaust memory, break delegation, or block production paths solely to create evidence.

For 20417, use an approved performance exercise only if needed. Record workload dirty-page rate, migration transport, network bandwidth, concurrent migrations, event message blackout value, external guest probe, and business objective. Microsoft calls the blackout unexpectedly long; the event is not itself a universal SLA threshold. Determine local notification priority from measured application impact.

Test scheduler skips, search-peer/index availability, lookup replication, role access, throttling, dashboard drilldowns, and notification routing. Keep `status=draft` until Microsoft-platform, virtualization, network/storage, workload, and Splunk owners accept supported versions, payload extraction, source health, fixture results, routing, and remediation procedure.

## Step 4 — Operationalize diagnosis rather than automatic retry

Responder sequence for 21502: (1) verify the raw VMMS/Admin record, record identity, host, event/index time, and source health; (2) identify the exact VM, source/destination, operation, operator/cluster action, error code, and related VMMS/Worker/cluster events; (3) check host patch/firmware and CPU/configuration compatibility; (4) compare virtual switches, network reachability, live-migration networks, firewall, performance option, and bandwidth; (5) verify Kerberos or CredSSP, SPNs, constrained delegation, and permissions according to the chosen topology; (6) verify destination memory/capacity, storage access, checkpoint/saved state, VM state, vTPM/shielding prerequisites, and simultaneous-migration limits; (7) apply an owner-approved correction; and (8) repeat only an authorized migration and validate guest/application continuity.

For 20417, verify the move really completed, identify source/destination and VM, compare the message blackout with external guest/service probes, inspect migration bandwidth and host CPU, transport choice, RDMA/SMB Multichannel where applicable, workload memory churn, and concurrent migrations. A completed move can still have user-visible impact. Route repeated long-blackout events to capacity/performance engineering.

Never invoke `Move-VM`, change `Set-VMHost`, purge Kerberos tickets, modify delegation/SPNs, create/rename switches, remove checkpoints, delete saved state, restart VMMS, drain a node, or retry a move directly from a Splunk alert. Several actions are disruptive or security-sensitive and require topology-specific review, maintenance, rollback, and workload validation.

Retain evidence according to incident/change and privacy policy. Messages can contain VM and host names; restrict access accordingly. Review source coverage, exceptions, event schema, and routing after Windows, Hyper-V, cluster, add-on, forwarder, authentication, network, storage, or migration-policy changes.

## Step 5 — Troubleshoot the detector separately from Hyper-V

- **No target events anywhere:** verify expected-host inventory, channel enabled state, WinEventLog input assignment, forwarder connectivity, index routing/retention, role access, source-type spelling, and known historical records. Absence is unknown, not healthy.
- **Event exists in Event Viewer but not Splunk:** compare channel path, stanza, disabled state, checkpoint, renderXml mode, source type, queues, index permissions, and event/index time.
- **Rows disappear after XML enablement:** search the observed `XmlWinEventLog:` source type, verify XML extraction, and use `$XmlRegex` for any XML ingest filter. Do not relabel XML blindly.
- **EventCode present but record identity null:** inspect raw event and add-on/extraction version. Keep a data-quality finding; `_cd` is only an index-local fallback.
- **Same incident pages twice:** compare native record identity, `_cd`, collection paths, dispatch overlap, and alert throttle. Preserve distinct record IDs.
- **Many 21502 records with different causes:** expected. Group by incident/change and message/error fingerprint only for triage; investigate each native payload.
- **20417 without known outage:** compare the raw blackout value with guest/application probes and local objective. It is still a documented long-blackout event, not proof of business outage.
- **21502 followed by success:** retain both. Close after destination ownership and guest/service validation; do not suppress historical failure.
- **Message parsing breaks after update or locale change:** fall back to EventCode and raw payload, update cohort-specific extraction tests, and avoid English-only regex as the alert gate.
grandmaExplanation: We watch for two Windows records: one says a live move of a virtual machine failed, and the other says the move finished but paused too long. The record starts an investigation; it does not tell us every cause or prove the application stayed available.
